transcript.text: Hello, South City Cycling Club.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: Oh, hi.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Er … I want to find out about joining the club.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: I can help you there.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: I’m the club secretary and my name’s Jim Hunter.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: Oh, hi Jim.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: So, are you interested in membership for yourself?
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: That’s right.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: Well there are basically two types of adult membership.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: If you’re pretty serious about cycling, there’s the Full membership.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: That costs 260 dollars and that covers you not just for ordinary cycling but also for races both here in the city and also in other parts of Australia.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Well, I’m not really up to that standard.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I was more interested in just joining a group to do some cycling in my free time.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Sure.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: That’s why most people join.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: So, in that case you’d be better with the Recreational membership.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: That’s 108 dollars if you’re over 19, and 95 dollars if you’re under.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: It’s paid quarterly, and you can upgrade it later to the Full membership if you want to, of course.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: Now both types of membership include the club fee of 20 dollars.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: They also provide insurance in case you have an accident, though we hope you won’t need that, of course.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: No.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: OK, well, I’ll go with the Recreational membership, I think.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: And that allows me to join in the club activities, and so on?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: That’s right.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: And once you’re a member of the club, you’re also permitted to wear our kit when you’re out cycling.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: It’s green and white.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: Yes, I’ve seen cyclists wearing it.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: So, can I buy that at the club?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: No, it’s made to order by a company in Brisbane.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: You can find them online: they’re called Jerriz.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: That’s J-E-R-R-I-Z.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: You can use your membership number to put in an order on their website.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Now, can you tell me a bit about the rides I can do?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Sure.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: So we have training rides pretty well every morning, and they’re a really good way of improving your cycling skills as well as your general level of fitness, but they’re different levels.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: Level A is pretty fast – you’re looking at about 30 or 35 kilometres an hour.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: If you can do about 25 kilometres an hour, you’d probably be level B, and then level C are the novices, who stay at about 15 kilometres per hour.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Well I reckon I’d be level B.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: So, when are the sessions for that level?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: There are a couple each week.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: They’re both early morning sessions.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: There’s one on Tuesdays, and for that one you meet at 5.30 am, and the meeting point’s the stadium – do you know where that is?
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: Yes, it’s quite near my home, in fact.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: OK, and how about the other one?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: That’s on Thursdays.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: It starts at the same time, but they meet at the main gate to the park.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: Is that the one just past the shopping mall?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: That’s it.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: So how long are the rides?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: They’re about an hour and a half.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: So, if you have a job it’s easy to fit in before you go to work.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: And the members often go somewhere for coffee afterwards, so it’s quite a social event.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: That sounds good.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I’ve only just moved to the city so I don’t actually know many people yet.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Well, it’s a great way to meet people.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: And does each ride have a leader?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Sometimes, but not always.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: But you don’t really need one; the group members on the ride support one another, anyway.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: How would we know where to go?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: If you check the club website, you’ll see that the route for each ride is clearly marked.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: So you can just print that out and take it along with you.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: It’s similar from one week to another, but it’s not always exactly the same.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: And what do I need to bring?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Well, bring a bottle of water, and your phone.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: You shouldn’t use if while you’re cycling, buy have it with you.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: And in winter, it’s well before sunrise when we set out, so you need to make sure your bike’s got lights.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: That’s OK.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Well, thanks Jim.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I’d definitely like to join.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: So what’s the best way of going about it?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: You can …
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: Thanks for coming everyone.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: OK, so this meeting is for new staff and staff who haven’t been involved with our volunteering projects yet.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: So basically, the idea is that we allow staff to give up some of their work time to help on various charity projects to benefit the local community.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We’ve been doing this for the last five years and it’s been very successful.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Participating doesn’t necessarily involve a huge time commitment.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The company will pay for eight hours of your time.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: That can be used over one or two days all at once, or spread over several months throughout the year.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: There are some staff who enjoy volunteering so much they also give up their own free time for a couple of hours every week.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: It’s completely up to you.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Obviously, many people will have family commitments and aren’t as available as other members of staff.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Feedback from staff has been overwhelmingly positive.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Because they felt they were doing something really useful, nearly everyone agreed that volunteering made them feel more motivated at work.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: They also liked building relationships with the people in the local community and felt valued by them.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: One or two people also said it was a good thing to have on their CVs.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: One particularly successful project last year was the Get Working Project.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: This was aimed at helping unemployed people in the area get back to work.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Our staff were able to help them improve their telephone skills, such as writing down messages and speaking with confidence to potential customers, which they had found quite difficult.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: This is something many employers look for in job applicants – and something we all do without even thinking about, every day at work.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We’ve got an exciting new project starting this year.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Up until now, we’ve mainly focused on projects to do with education and training.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: And we’ll continue with our reading project in schools and our work with local charities.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: But we’ve also agreed to help out on a conservation project in Redfern Park.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: So if any of you fancy being outside and getting your hands dirty, this is the project for you.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: I also want to mention the annual Digital Inclusion Day, which is coming up next month.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The aim of this is to help older people keep up with technology.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: And this year, instead of hosting the event in our own training facility, we’re using the ICT suite at Hill College, as it can hold far more people.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We’ve invited over 60 people from the Silver Age Community Centre to take part, so we’ll need a lot of volunteers to help with this event.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: If you’re interested in taking part, please go to the volunteering section of our website and complete the relevant form.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We won’t be providing any training for this but you’ll be paired with an experienced volunteer if you’ve never done it before.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: By the way, don’t forget to tell your manager about any volunteering activities you decide to do.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The participants on the Digital Inclusion Day really benefited.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The majority were in their seventies, though some were younger and a few were even in their nineties!
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Quite a few owned both a computer and a mobile phone, but these tended to be outdated models. They generally knew how to do simple things, like send texts, but weren’t aware of recent developments in mobile phone technology. A few were keen to learn but most were quite dismissive at first – they couldn’t see the point of updating their skills.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: But that soon changed.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The feedback was very positive.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The really encouraging thing was that participants all said they felt much more confident about using social media to keep in touch with their grandchildren, who prefer this form of communication to phoning or sending emails. A lot of them also said playing online games would help them make new friends and keep their brains active.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: They weren’t that impressed with being able to order their groceries online, as they liked going out to the shops, but some said it would come in handy if they were ill or the weather was really bad.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: One thing they asked about was using tablets for things like reading newspapers – some people had been given tablets as presents but had never used them, so that’s something we’ll make sure we include this time …
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Ah … come in, Russ.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Thank you.
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: Now you wanted to consult me about your class presentation on nanotechnology – you’re due to give it in next week, aren’t you?
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: That’s right.
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: And I’m really struggling.
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: I chose the topic because I didn’t know much about it and wanted to learn more, but now I’ve read so much about it, in a way there’s too much to say – I could talk for much longer than the twenty minutes I’ve been allocated.
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: Should I assume the other students don’t know much, and give them a kind of general introduction, or should I try and make them share my fascination with a particular aspect?
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: You could do either, but you’ll need to have it clear in your own mind.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Then I think I’ll give an overview.
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Now, one way of approaching this is to work through developments in chronological order.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Uh-huh.
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: On the other hand, you could talk about the numerous ways that nanotechnology is being applied.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: You mean things like thin films on camera displays to make them water-repellent, and additives to make motorcycle helmets stronger and lighter.
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: Exactly.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Or another way would be to focus on its impact in one particular area, say medicine, or space exploration.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: That would make it easier to focus.
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: Perhaps I should do that.
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: I think that would be a good idea.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: How important is it to include slides in the presentation?
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: They aren’t essential, by any means.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: And there’s a danger of tailoring what you say to fit whatever slides you can find.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: While it can be good to include slides, you could end up spending too long looking for suitable ones.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: You might find it better to leave them out.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: I see.
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: Another thing I was wondering about was how to start.
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: I know presentations often begin with ‘First I’m going to talk about this, and then I’ll talk about that’, but I thought about asking the audience what they know about nanotechnology.
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: That would be fine if you had an hour or two for the presentation, but you might find that you can’t do anything with the answers you get, and it simply eats into the short time that’s available.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: So, maybe I should mention a particular way that nanotechnology is used, to focus people’s attention.
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: That sounds sensible.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: What do you think I should do next?
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: I really have to plan the presentation today and tomorrow.
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: Well, initially I think you should ignore all the notes you’ve made, take a small piece of paper, and write a single short sentence that ties together the whole presentation: it can be something as simple as ‘Nanotechnology is already improving our lives’.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Then start planning the content around that.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: You can always modify that sentence later, if you need to.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: OK, now let’s think about actually giving the presentation.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: You’ve only given one before, if I remember correctly, about an experiment you’d been involved in.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: That’s right.
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: It was pretty rubbish!
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: Let’s say it was better in some respects than in others.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: With regard to the structure.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: I felt that you ended rather abruptly, without rounding it off.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Be careful not to do that in next week’s presentation.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: And you made very little eye contact with the audience, because you were looking down at your notes most of the time.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: You need to be looking at the audience and only occasionally glancing at your notes.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Mmm.
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: Your body language was a little odd.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Every time you showed a slide, you turned your back on the audience so you could look at it – you should have been looking at your laptop.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: And you kept scratching your head, so I found myself wondering when you were next going to do that, instead of listening to what you were saying!
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Oh dear.
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: What did you think of the language?
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: I knew that not everyone was familiar with the subject, so I tried to make it as simple as I could.
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: Yes, that came across.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: You used a few words that are specific to the field, but you always explained what they meant, so the audience wouldn’t have had any difficulty understanding.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Uh-huh.
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: I must say the handouts you prepared were well thought out.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: They were a good summary of your presentation, which people would be able to refer to later on.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: So well done on that.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Thank you.
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: Well, I hope that helps you with next week’s presentation.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Yes, it will.
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: Thanks a lot.
transcript.speaker: RUSS

transcript.text: I’ll look forward to seeing a big improvement, then.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Today, we’ll be continuing the series of lectures on memory by focusing on what is called episodic memory and what can happen if this is not working properly.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Episodic memory refers to the memory of an event or ‘episode’.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Episodic memories allow us to mentally travel back in time to an event from the past.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Episodic memories include various details about these events, for example, when an event happened and other information such as the location.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: To help understand this concept, try to remember the last time you ate dinner at a restaurant.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The ability to remember where you ate, who you were with and the items you ordered are all features of an episodic memory.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Episodic memory is distinct from another type of memory called semantic memory.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This is the type of factual memory that we have in common with everyone else – that is your general knowledge of the world.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: To build upon a previous example, remembering where you parked your car is an example of episodic memory, but your understanding of what a car is and how an engine works are examples of sematic memory.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Unlike episodic memory, semantic memory isn’t dependent on recalling personal experiences.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Episodic memory can be thought of as a process with several different steps of memory processing: encoding, consolidation and retrieval.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The initial step is called encoding.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This involves the process of receiving and registering information, which is necessary for creating memories of information or events that you experience.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The degree to which you can successfully encode information depends on the level of attention you give to an event while it’s actually happening.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Being distracted can make effective encoding very difficult.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Encoding of episodic memories is also influenced by how you process the event.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: For example, if you were introduced to someone called Charlie, you might make the connection that your uncle has the same name.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Future recollection of Charlie’s name is much easier if you have a strategy to help you encode it.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Memory consolidation, the next step in forming an episodic memory, is the process by which memories of encoded information are strengthened, stabilised and stored to facilitate later retrieval.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Consolidation is most effective when the information being stored can be linked to an existing network of information.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Consolidation makes it possible for you to store memories for later retrieval indefinitely.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Forming strong memories depends on the frequency with which you try to retrieve them.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Memories can fade or become harder to retrieve if they aren’t used very often.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The last step in forming episodic memories is called retrieval, which is the conscious recollection of encoded information.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Retrieving information from episodic memory depends upon semantic, olfactory, auditory and visual factors.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: These help episodic memory retrieval by acting as a prompt.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: For example, when recalling where you parked your car you may use the colour of a sign close to where you parked.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: You actually have to mentally travel back to the moment you parked.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: There are a wide range of neurological diseases and conditions that can affect episodic memory.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: These range from Alzheimer’s to schizophrenia to autism.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: An impairment of episodic memory can have a profound effect on individuals’ lives.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: For example, the symptoms of schizophrenia can be reasonably well controlled by medication; however, patients’ episodic memory may still be impaired and so they are often unable to return to university or work.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Recent studies have shown that computer- assisted games designed to keep the brain active can help improve their episodic memory.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Episodic memories can help people connect with others, for instance by sharing intimate details about their past; something individuals with autism often have problems with.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This may be caused by an absence of a sense of self.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This is essential for the storage of episodic memory, and has been found to be impaired in children with autism.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Research has shown that treatments that improve memory may also have a positive impact on children’s social development.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER
